progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B9: dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, carrier; each gamete gets one allele; the 2 x 2 square; a ratio is a chance per offspring; pedigree symbols and numbering; "Hidden in the parents: recessive. Hidden in the child: dominant." with its assumptions. From B10: X and Y; a male's single X; "Dad gives his X to daughters and his Y to sons"; "of all children" against "of sons"; X-linked recessive pedigree pattern and the rule-out; "Incomplete is in-between. Co shows both." Year 10: multiply for "and" (introduced in one sentence in Q1 as each birth being a separate chance). Not assumed: conditional probability (Q3 explains it as crossing out the box the person cannot be), X-linked dominant (not used).
progression.startsWith: The hook: Inheritance questions in the HSC rarely use peas. They give you an animal you haven't met, or a family where the pattern isn't obvious, and ask for a probability, or for what the evidence can and can't tell you.
progression.stopsAfter: choosing incomplete dominance from a third phenotype and predicting a 1:2:1 cross and a two-birth probability; explaining why tortoiseshell cats are almost always female and finding sex-specific and overall probabilities in an X-linked cross; finding a 2/3 carrier chance and a 1/6 child probability across two families, then updating to 1/4 on new evidence; ruling out X-linked recessive with named individuals, explaining why autosomal dominant and recessive both fit, and judging which is more likely for a rare condition.
progression.nextLesson: population frequencies and SNP evidence (route entry bio-m5-b11).

teaching.task: When a cross or a family tree is new to you, how do you choose the model, find the probability, and say what the evidence can and cannot prove?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why some chicks are black and white (the heterozygous parents each pass one allele; the alleles separate, they did not blend) (2b); why multiply (each chick is a separate fertilisation) (2c); why tortoiseshell needs two X chromosomes (both alleles must be present) (3b); why sons cannot get the father's X (he gives sons his Y) (3c); why the man is a certain carrier (his mother could only give a recessive allele) (4b); why 2/3 (the woman cannot be the affected box, leaving three equally likely boxes) (4c); why the second child's chance changes (an affected child proves she is a carrier) (4d); why X-linked recessive fails (an affected mother would have only affected sons) (5b); why both autosomal patterns fit (no giveaway trio) (5c); why dominant is more likely (recessive needs two unrelated carriers for a rare allele) (5d).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on the hook (hook), then works through q1-question (question 1: Andalusian chickens), q1-model (choose the model, fill the square), q1-chance (two chicks, then only blue), q1-mistake (the classic mistake), q2-question (question 2: tortoiseshell cats) and the remaining scenes in order, with each reasoning stage shown on its own cue; ends with the unseen attempt (10 second countdown), brief feedback, the decision rule or board, and the key notes.
teaching.openingDecision: Inheritance questions in the HSC rarely use peas. They give you an animal you haven't met, or a family where the pattern isn't obvious, and ask for a probability, or for what the evidence can and can't tell you.
teaching.understandingCheck: Four, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a, 5a). The type badge is hidden during each hold in Q1 and Q2 because it names the model.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, BIO12-12, programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json, B5-IQ4-02, p 49): "model the formation of new combinations of genotypes produced during meiosis, including but not limited to:" with "interpreting examples of autosomal, sex-linkage, co-dominance, incomplete dominance and multiple alleles (ACSBL085)" and "constructing and interpreting information and data from pedigrees and Punnett squares". Practice and transfer: ledger rows p1058 and p1059 stay with B9 and B10; G02 adds the practice row and the two items B9 deferred here (the 2/3 conditional probability and choosing between competing modes).

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in the G03c layout: top-left the short task line; under it the stimulus (painted organism plates or a pedigree); under that the grouped givens card; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Incomplete dominance", "X-linked", "Pedigree: probability", "Pedigree: which pattern?"). A first-moves strip on the far left carries three rows: "1 choose the model", "2 write the genotypes you are sure of", "3 combine the chances" and ticks the row each scene uses; it dims to an outline during every countdown. Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Pedigrees use B9's data-driven Pedigree (standard symbols only, Roman numerals, individual numbers); no people, faces or bodies.
design.transitionPlan: One practice board persists: the question card at the top left, the working area below it. Each question clears the area, writes on its stimulus (square or pedigree) and then builds one reasoning stage per scene, with the classic-mistake chip crossed out at the end; the decision board gathers the four methods before the notes; scene crossfade with settle.
